Week 87: A Week That Nearly Balanced

Courts blocked the president repeatedly while he threatened electoral refusal, press bans, and coerced loyalty payments in return.

The clock had barely moved in a week that felt anything but still. Week 87 opened with the Speaker of the House declaring, in plain terms, that his party would not let an elected Democratic majority take power. It closed with the president banning three news organizations from the White House grounds. In between came court rulings that blocked him, legislation that armed him, and a widening fracture inside his own party over rhetoric even some Republicans called bigotry. The Democracy Clock recorded all of it. The arithmetic came out close to even.

At the end of last week, the clock stood at 7:35 p.m. It closed this week at the same time, a net movement of less than a minute. That stillness was not calm. It was cancellation. Genuine judicial pushback, concentrated and repeated, offset a dense pile-up of executive threats, disinformation, and institutional avoidance. The traits pulled hard in both directions. For once, the ledger nearly balanced.

The week's most direct threat to the constitutional order came early. Speaker Mike Johnson said plainly that Republicans would not accept a Democratic House majority, regardless of how the midterms turned out. Retired judge J. Michael Luttig, a conservative long respected across party lines, followed with a specific warning: the House could replace its clerk to block Democratic members from being seated. This was not vague grievance. It was a described mechanism. Luttig called Trump the greatest threat to the coming election, and he did not appear to be exaggerating for effect.

Democrats answered by promising oversight if they won anyway, unveiling plans to investigate family enrichment, pardons, and enforcement conduct. It was a modest countermeasure against a serious threat. The imbalance between the two sides captured something essential about the week: a specific plan to nullify an election, set against a promise to investigate if allowed to govern. One side held the tools of refusal. The other held only the tools of promise.

Alongside that threat sat a second, more personal use of power. Trump tied public money to loyalty. He linked a proposed $5,000 payment to Republican control of Congress. He threatened to withhold federal disaster aid from North Carolina unless voters backed his chosen candidate, then called the threat a joke. He also waged a running battle over the Kennedy Center, threatening first to block a $257 million renovation, then to demolish the building outright, unless his name was placed on it. The center's board, stacked with his allies, obliged him by voting to close the building rather than renovate it under the court order that blocked his name. He pressured South Dakota's governor about adding his likeness to Mount Rushmore. None of this was subtle. Public institutions became bargaining chips for personal tribute.

Here the courts intervened, and intervened repeatedly. The Supreme Court rejected Trump's mail-in ballot restrictions ahead of the midterms. It blocked his attempt to fire a Federal Reserve governor. It struck down his birthright citizenship rules and his sweeping tariffs. A federal judge separately blocked the Kennedy Center's board from renaming the venue, prompting the closure standoff described above. Congress, in its own act of resistance, passed a war powers resolution directing Trump to end hostilities in Iran, the third such vote this term. These were not symbolic gestures. They were binding checks, and they held.

Yet even as courts constrained him, Congress handed him new power. Lawmakers passed a sanctions bill granting the president sweeping tariff authority over countries buying Russian oil. This broad grant of trade power passed the same week the Supreme Court struck down his prior tariffs. The pattern was almost circular. The judiciary closes one door. The legislature opens another.

Immigration enforcement deepened its human cost this week. The administration ended Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitian nationals, triggering ankle monitoring, mass detentions in Springfield, and reporting that linked the policy to a student's suicide. A newly expanded public-charge rule threatened to deny green cards based on benefits use, drawing lawsuits from twenty-two states and the District of Columbia, along with a separate suit from six major cities. The legal resistance was substantial. The human toll, already inflicted, was not something a lawsuit could undo.

DHS, meanwhile, was caught inflating the scale of a supposed threat. The agency claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 non-citizen voters in Nevada. It could verify only 185, an overstatement of roughly eighty-five times. A whistleblower separately alleged the agency told officers to search voter databases in ways that might break state law, and that they would face no personal liability for doing so. Civil rights groups sued over armed ICE presence near polling places, invoking a nineteenth-century statute meant to prevent exactly this kind of intimidation. Inflated fraud claims paired with real intimidation tactics. The two reinforced each other regardless of the truth of either.

A separate and uglier current ran through the week's campaign politics. A Texas Republican candidate's viral, xenophobic post about Asian students drew condemnation from Senators Cornyn and Cruz, Governor Abbott, and strategist Karl Rove, who broke with three decades of Republican-only endorsements to back the Democrat instead. The candidate doubled down rather than retreating. He was not alone. Other Republican candidates were exposed for Nazi-sympathetic social media content, ties to a 2017 white supremacist rally, and a deleted tribute to a relative's service in the German military. Reporting also surfaced an organized network with neo-Nazi ties operating inside mainstream conservative institutions. The condemnations were real. So was the refusal, in several cases, to back down.

Elsewhere in the party, a rare convergence took shape around artificial intelligence. The heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind, along with Elon Musk, publicly called for a coordinated slowdown in AI development, warning of catastrophic risk. Bernie Sanders introduced legislation to ban artificial superintelligence outright. Trump dismissed the warnings as a hoax akin to climate denial, and senior advisers echoed him, framing the calls for caution as self-interested liability avoidance. An Anthropic researcher resigned publicly, warning of a world in peril. It was one of the few moments this term where industry and a former president found more common ground with each other than with the sitting administration.

Congress used its remaining days before recess unevenly. The House voted to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt for defying Epstein-related subpoenas, a rare and unanimous assertion of legislative power against elite non-cooperation. But Speaker Johnson then canceled votes and sent members home until after the midterms, avoiding a scheduled vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Hegseth and further war powers accountability. Accountability advanced in one chamber and evaporated in another, sometimes within the same week.

Money and law intersected again in the fight over cryptocurrency regulation. Senator Lummis's revised ethics bill included a blind-trust loophole and a grandfathering provision that would have let Trump retain his personal crypto holdings, including sponsorship revenue, while nominally complying with new rules. The Senate ultimately blocked the bill on a narrow vote, a modest check on legislation designed, in part, to protect the president's own finances. Trump separately pursued a stock-trading ban for lawmakers that would have exempted himself.

The week's clearest attack on the press came at its end. Trump formally banned CNN, MSNBC, and Politico from the White House, citing their coverage. It marked an unprecedented step beyond the administration's prior pattern of targeting individual reporters. The ban unfolded alongside a $400 million super PAC advertising campaign built on false claims about opponents' records, and a website marketed as a voter registration checker that was found to be harvesting personal data for resale. Separately, the Pentagon was shown to have hidden the true scope of casualties and base damage from the Iran war, keeping the public in the dark about an active conflict's real cost.

Not every thread pointed toward erosion. A federal judge blocked DHS from threatening a citizen with prosecution for criticizing immigration enforcement, a narrow but real defense of speech rights. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates despite open presidential pressure not to, an assertion of institutional independence in monetary policy. The Justice Department won substantial antitrust relief against Google. These were not dramatic reversals. But they were real, and they mattered.

Congress has already passed, and Trump has already signed, the sanctions and tariff bill granting him new trade power over countries buying Russian energy. The war powers resolution passed by the House awaits a Senate response that has not yet come. Both threads carry into whatever comes next, unresolved.

The week's near-stillness on the clock should not be mistaken for a quiet one. It was a week of open threats to the electoral transition, offset by courts that still functioned; of racist rhetoric that drew real condemnation but not always retraction; of an administration willing to concede almost nothing except when forced. The balance held this week. Nothing here suggests it will hold indefinitely.
